summary: Specifies how to map the Real-time Transport Protocol onto the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol, along with how to signal it with SDP. DCCP offers congestion control for real-time applications. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary:
DCCP is a transport protocol that delivers packets without guaranteeing they arrive, but that does control how fast you send them, so the network does not fill up. That makes it a good match for live audio and video, which is what RTP carries.

This RFC says exactly how RTP rides on DCCP: one media packet per datagram, control reports in their own datagrams, and a session description that tells the other end which transport and port to use. It also says how the session should be adjusted when the network slows the sender down.

questions: how to run rtp over dccp
what port does rtp over dccp use
how to signal dccp in sdp
subtitle: Carrying live media over DCCP, a transport that adds congestion control to unreliable delivery.

tldr.problem: RTP is widely used for real-time media but most applications built on it do not control their sending rate, which risks congestion collapse. Running RTP over TCP is not an option for interactive media because TCP is reliable and slow to adapt.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC puts each RTP packet in one DCCP datagram and each compound RTCP packet in another, so the transport's congestion control governs the media rate. SDP gains new protocol identifiers, a new service-code attribute and a registered port.
tldr.outcome: Applications get congestion control from the operating system instead of writing their own. The RFC was later updated by RFC 6773, which adds a UDP encapsulation for DCCP for NAT traversal.

facts.label: Keepalive interval
facts.value: A zero-length DCCP-Data packet once every 15 seconds

facts.label: Default DCCP port
facts.value: 5004, with 5005 registered for a separate RTCP connection

today: RFC 5762 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, and it was updated by RFC 6773, which adds a UDP encapsulation for DCCP for NAT traversal.

sections.title: What This RFC Specifies
sections.content:
The Real-time Transport Protocol is widely used in video streaming, telephony and other real-time networked applications. RTP can run over a range of lower-layer transport protocols, and the performance of an application using RTP is heavily influenced by the choice of lower-layer transport. DCCP is a transport protocol that provides desirable properties for real-time applications running on unmanaged best-effort IP networks.

This memo describes how RTP can be framed for transport using DCCP and discusses some of the implications of such a framing. It also describes how the Session Description Protocol can be used to signal such sessions. The structure of the memo is: a rationale in Section 2, the conventions used in Section 3, the definition of how RTP packets are framed within DCCP in Section 4, the associated signalling in Section 5, security considerations in Section 6, and IANA considerations in Section 7.

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: The document has two halves: how the packets are packed for DCCP, and how a session description announces that setup. The requirement words tell an implementer which rules are mandatory.

sections.title: Why Map RTP onto DCCP
sections.content:
With the widespread adoption of RTP have come concerns that many real-time applications do not implement congestion control, leading to the potential for congestion collapse of the network. The designers of RTP recognised the issue, stating in RFC 3551 that if best-effort service is being used, RTP receivers SHOULD monitor packet loss to ensure the loss rate stays within acceptable parameters, and that this condition can be satisfied by implementing congestion control mechanisms to adapt the transmission rate, or by arranging for a receiver to leave the session if the loss rate is unacceptably high.

While the goals are clear, the development of TCP friendly congestion control usable with RTP and real-time media applications is an open research question with many proposals for new algorithms but little deployment experience.

Two approaches have been used to provide congestion control for RTP. The first is to develop RTP extensions that incorporate congestion control, for example by extending RTP with feedback information so that TCP Friendly Rate Control can be implemented at the application level. That allows congestion control to be added to existing applications without operating system or network support, and offers the flexibility to experiment with new algorithms as they are developed. Unfortunately, it also passes the complexity of implementing congestion control onto application authors, a burden many would prefer to avoid.

The second approach is to run RTP on a lower-layer transport protocol that provides congestion control. One possibility is RTP over TCP, but the reliable nature of TCP and the dynamics of its congestion control algorithm make it inappropriate for most interactive real-time applications; SCTP is inappropriate for similar reasons. A better fit may be RTP over DCCP, since DCCP offers unreliable packet delivery and a choice of congestion control. This gives applications the ability to tailor the transport to their needs and take advantage of better congestion control algorithms as they become available, while passing the complexity of implementation to the operating system.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to add congestion control to live media. Either the application does it itself, using extra feedback messages, or the transport does it. The second is simpler for application writers, so the RFC defines how to put RTP on top of a transport that already has congestion control.

sections.title: RTP Data Packets on DCCP
sections.content:
Each RTP data packet MUST be conveyed in a single DCCP datagram. Fields in the RTP header MUST be interpreted according to the RTP specification and any applicable RTP profile and payload format. Header processing is not affected by DCCP framing; in particular, the semantics of the RTP sequence number and the DCCP sequence number are not compatible, and the value of one cannot be inferred from the other.

A DCCP connection is opened when an end system joins an RTP session and remains open for the duration of the session. To ensure NAT bindings are kept open, an end system SHOULD send a zero-length DCCP-Data packet once every 15 seconds during periods when it has no other data to send. This removes the need for RTP no-op packets and similar application-level keepalives. It is not needed if it is known that the DCCP congestion control in use provides a transport-level keepalive, or if the application can determine that there are no NAT devices on the path.

RTP data packets MUST obey the dictates of DCCP congestion control. In some cases congestion control will require a sender to send at a rate below that which the payload format would otherwise use. To support this, an application could use either a rate-adaptive payload format or a range of payload formats, allowing it to switch to a lower rate format if necessary. RTP extensions that provide application-level congestion control will conflict with DCCP congestion control and MUST NOT be used.

DCCP allows an application to choose the checksum coverage, using a partial checksum to allow an application to receive packets with corrupt payloads. Some RTP payload formats can make use of this in conjunction with payload-specific mechanisms to improve performance in environments with frequent non-congestive packet corruption. If such a payload format is used, an RTP end system MAY enable partial checksums at the DCCP layer, in which case the checksum MUST cover at least the DCCP and RTP headers to ensure packets are correctly delivered. Partial checksums MUST NOT be used unless supported by mechanisms in the RTP payload format.
sections.plainLanguage: One media packet travels in one datagram, and the two sequence numbers mean different things, so one cannot be read from the other. The transport's own keepalive replaces the empty media packets some applications send. The sender must slow down when the transport says the network is congested, and must not also run its own congestion control on top.

sections.title: RTP Control Packets
sections.content:
The RTP Control Protocol is used in the standard manner with DCCP. RTCP packets are grouped into compound packets and each compound RTCP packet is transported in a single DCCP datagram.

The usual RTCP timing rules apply, with the additional constraint that RTCP packets MUST obey the DCCP congestion control algorithm negotiated for the connection. This can prevent a participant from sending an RTCP packet at the expiration of the RTCP transmission timer if there is insufficient network capacity available. In such cases the RTCP packet is delayed and sent at the earliest possible instant when capacity becomes available, and the actual time the packet was sent is then used as the basis for calculating the next RTCP transmission time.

RTCP packets comprise only a small fraction of the total traffic in an RTP session, so delays in their transmission due to congestion control are not expected to be common, provided the configured nominal session bandwidth is in line with the bandwidth achievable on the DCCP connection. If the capacity of the DCCP connection is significantly below the nominal session bandwidth, RTCP packets may be delayed enough for participants to time out due to apparent inactivity. In such cases the session parameters SHOULD be re-negotiated to more closely match the available capacity, for example by performing a re-invite with an updated bandwidth line when using SIP for signalling. Since the nominal session bandwidth is chosen based on media codec capabilities, a session where the nominal bandwidth is much larger than the available bandwidth will likely become unusable because of constraints on the media channel, before it becomes unusable because of constraints on the RTCP channel.

There is the potential for overlap between information conveyed in RTCP packets and that conveyed in DCCP acknowledgement options. In general this is not an issue, since RTCP packets contain media-specific data that is not present in DCCP acknowledgement options, and DCCP options contain network-level data that is not present in RTCP. There is no overlap between the five RTCP packet types defined in the RTP specification and the standard DCCP options. There are, however, cases where overlap does occur, most clearly between the Loss RLE Report Blocks defined as part of the RTCP Extended Reports and the DCCP Ack Vector option. If there is overlap between RTCP report packets and DCCP acknowledgements, an application SHOULD use either RTCP feedback or DCCP acknowledgements, but not both; using both wastes available network capacity but is not otherwise harmful.
sections.plainLanguage: Control reports follow the usual rules, except that they also wait for the transport's permission to send. If the session was set up for more bandwidth than the link can carry, the parameters should be renegotiated rather than letting participants time out. Sending both RTCP feedback and DCCP acknowledgements is wasteful, so pick one.

sections.title: Multiplexing Data and Control
sections.content: The obvious mapping of RTP onto DCCP creates two DCCP connections for each RTP flow: one for RTP data packets and one for RTP control packets. A frequent criticism of RTP relates to the number of ports it uses, since large telephony gateways can support more than 32768 RTP flows between pairs of gateways and so run out of UDP ports. In addition, use of multiple ports complicates NAT traversal. For these reasons, it is RECOMMENDED that the RTP and RTCP traffic for a single RTP session is multiplexed onto a single DCCP connection following the guidelines of RFC 5761, where possible. It may not be possible in all circumstances, for example when translating from an RTP stream over a non-DCCP transport that uses conflicting RTP payload types and RTCP packet types.
sections.plainLanguage: Without multiplexing, every call needs two connections. Carrying both media and control on one connection avoids running out of ports on large gateways and makes NAT traversal simpler, so the RFC recommends it.

sections.title: RTP Sessions, Connections and Profiles
sections.content:
An end system SHOULD NOT assume that it will observe only a single RTP synchronisation source because it is using DCCP framing. An RTP session can span any number of transport connections and can include RTP mixers or translators bringing other participants into the session. The use of a unicast DCCP connection does not imply that the RTP session will have only two participants, and RTP end systems SHOULD assume that multiple synchronisation sources may be observed when using RTP over DCCP, unless otherwise signalled.

An RTP translator bridging multiple DCCP connections to form a single RTP session needs to be aware of the congestion state of each DCCP connection, and must adapt the media to the available capacity of each. The Codec Control Messages defined in the AVPF profile may be used to signal congestion state to the media senders, allowing them to adapt their transmission. Alternatively, media transcoding may be used to perform adaptation, which is computationally expensive, induces delay and generally gives poor-quality results. Depending on the payload, it might also be possible to use some form of scalable coding.

A single RTP session may also span a DCCP connection and some other type of transport connection, for example an RTP over DCCP connection from an end system to an RTP translator with an RTP over UDP and IP multicast group on the other side, or an RTP over DCCP connection linking PSTN gateways. The issues for such a translator are similar to those when linking two DCCP connections, except that the congestion control algorithms on either side may not be compatible. Implementation of effective translators for such an environment is non-trivial.

In general there is no conflict between new RTP profiles and DCCP framing, and most RTP profiles can be negotiated for use over DCCP, with two exceptions. An RTP profile that is intolerant of packet corruption may conflict with the DCCP partial checksum feature; the integrity protection provided by the RTP/SAVP profile is an example and cannot be used with DCCP partial checksums. An RTP profile that mandates a particular non-DCCP lower-layer transport will conflict with DCCP. Profiles that fall under these exceptions SHOULD NOT be used with DCCP unless the conflicting features can be disabled. Of the profiles currently defined, the audio and video profile with minimal control, the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol, the Extended RTP profile for RTCP-based feedback and the Extended Secure RTP profile for RTCP-based feedback MAY be used with DCCP, noting the potential conflict between DCCP partial checksums and the integrity protection provided by the secure RTP variants.
sections.plainLanguage: One DCCP connection does not mean a two-party call. A session can span several connections and mixers, so an endpoint must expect several audio sources. Most RTP profiles work over DCCP, but a profile that needs every bit intact cannot be combined with partial checksums.

sections.title: Signalling RTP over DCCP with SDP
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol and the offer/answer model are widely used to negotiate RTP sessions, for example using SIP. SDP uses a media line to convey details of the media format and transport protocol used. The proto field denotes the transport protocol and the port indicates the transport port to which the media is sent. The memo defines five values of the proto field for media transported using DCCP: DCCP, DCCP/RTP/AVP, DCCP/RTP/SAVP, DCCP/RTP/AVPF and DCCP/RTP/SAVPF.

The DCCP identifier is similar to the UDP and TCP identifiers and denotes the DCCP transport protocol but not its upper-layer protocol. An SDP media line specifying DCCP MUST further qualify the application-layer protocol using a fmt identifier. A single DCCP port is used, as denoted by the port field. The DCCP identifier MUST NOT be used to signal RTP sessions running over DCCP; those sessions MUST use an identifier of the form DCCP/RTP/.... The four other identifiers name RTP running over DCCP with, respectively, the audio and video profile with minimal control, the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol, the Extended RTP profile for RTCP-based feedback and the Extended Secure RTP profile for RTCP-based feedback. RTP payload formats used with those identifiers MUST use the payload type number as their fmt value, and if the payload type number is dynamically assigned an additional rtpmap attribute MUST be included.

DCCP port 5004 is registered for use by the RTP profiles listed, and SHOULD be the default port chosen by applications using them. If multiple RTP sessions are active from a host, even-numbered ports in the dynamic range SHOULD be used for the other sessions. If RTCP is to be sent on a separate DCCP connection to RTP, the RTCP connection SHOULD use the next higher destination port number, unless an alternative DCCP port is signalled using the a=rtcp: attribute, which SHOULD be used whenever an alternate port is used.

In addition to the port number, a DCCP connection has an associated service code, signalled with a new SDP attribute dccp-service-code, which may be written in hexadecimal, decimal or ASCII form; a parser MUST interpret service codes according to their numeric value regardless of the form used. Five service codes are registered for RTP: SC:RTPA for an RTP session conveying audio data, SC:RTPV for video, SC:RTPT for text media, SC:RTPO for any other type of media, and SC:RTCP for an RTCP connection separate from the corresponding RTP. To ease the job of middleboxes, applications SHOULD use these service codes, and the service code SHOULD match the top-level media type signalled for the session.

The a=setup: attribute indicates which endpoint should initiate the DCCP connection establishment, and MUST be used in a manner comparable with TCP-based media transport. The a=connection: attribute MUST be used in a compatible manner to decide whether a new DCCP connection needs to be established after a subsequent offer/answer exchange. A single DCCP connection can be used to transport multiplexed RTP and RTCP packets, and such multiplexing MUST be signalled using an a=rtcp-mux attribute. If multiplexed RTP and RTCP are not to be used, the a=rtcp-mux attribute MUST NOT be present in the SDP offer and a separate DCCP connection MUST be opened for the RTCP data on a different port.
sections.plainLanguage: The session description names the transport in the media line, gives the port, and adds an attribute carrying the DCCP service code. The service code tells middleboxes what kind of traffic the connection carries, which is why the RFC asks applications to set it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations in the RTP specification and any applicable RTP profile or payload format apply when transporting RTP over DCCP, as do the security considerations in the DCCP specification. The SDP signalling described in Section 5 is subject to the security considerations of the Session Description Protocol, the offer/answer model, TCP-based media transport, RTP over TCP and the RTP multiplexing specification.

The provision of effective congestion control for RTP through use of DCCP is expected to help reduce the potential for denial of service present when RTP flows ignore the advice in the RTP specification to monitor packet loss and reduce their sending rate in the face of persistent congestion.

There is a potential conflict between the Secure RTP profiles and the DCCP partial checksum option, since those profiles introduce and recommend the use of message authentication for RTP and RTCP packets. Message authentication codes of the type used by these profiles cannot be used with partial checksums, since any bit error in the DCCP packet payload will cause the authentication check to fail. Accordingly, DCCP partial checksums SHOULD NOT be used in conjunction with SRTP authentication. The confidentiality features of the basic RTP specification cannot be used with DCCP partial checksums, since bit errors propagate. Despite the fact that bit errors do not propagate when using AES in counter mode, the Secure RTP profiles SHOULD NOT be used with DCCP partial checksums, since the profiles require authentication for security and authentication is incompatible with partial checksums.
sections.plainLanguage: Authenticated RTP and partial checksums cannot be combined: a partial checksum deliberately accepts a damaged packet, and an authentication tag cannot tell a damaged packet from a forged one. The RFC asks that SRTP profiles not be used with partial checksums.

viz.caption: THE FRAMING RULES FOR RTP DATA PACKETS

items.title: One packet per datagram
items.text: Each RTP data packet travels in a single DCCP datagram.

items.title: Keep the binding open
items.text: Send a zero-length DCCP-Data packet once every 15 seconds when there is nothing else to send, so NAT bindings stay open.

items.title: Obey the transport
items.text: Data packets must obey DCCP congestion control, so the sender may have to use a lower rate than the payload format would allow.

items.title: No second congestion controller
items.text: RTP extensions that provide application-level congestion control must not be used alongside DCCP.

items.title: Partial checksums need payload support
items.text: They may only be used when the payload format has matching mechanisms, and must still cover the DCCP and RTP headers.
